This page goes with **Chapter 35, Minimalism** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Minimalism.html). Read each section there first.
All patterns here are made up for the page; none is copied from a piece.

## 35.1 Additive process

Philip Glass's early pieces such as *Two Pages* and *Music in Fifths* (both 1969, the book says) change a repeating pattern by adding or taking away
a note at a time. The book also names the pulsing chords of *Einstein on the Beach* (Act 1, Scene 1, "Train"), where each chord is stretched by adding
subdivisions. ([Two Pages on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Glass+Two+Pages), [Music in Fifths](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Glass+Music+in+Fifths).)
Below, a pattern can grow, shrink, or lose notes from the front. Watch the rows: each is one step of the process.

::: {.pt data-pt="additive"}
:::

## 35.2 Phase shifting

Steve Reich found that two tape loops of the same sound, running at almost the same speed, slide out of step and slowly back in
(*It's Gonna Rain*, 1965; *Come Out*, 1966). He then had live players do it: *Piano Phase* and *Violin Phase* (1967) and *Clapping Music* (1972).
([Piano Phase](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Reich+Piano+Phase), [Clapping Music](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Reich+Clapping+Music).)
In the stepped way one player holds steady while the other moves one note ahead, repeats, moves again, until the two are back together.
The player offers a steady drift too (the second voice a hair faster), which is how the loops behaved.

::: {.pt data-pt="phasing"}
:::

The table under the rings is the *rotation* the book draws: line 2 starts on the second note, line 3 on the third, until the pattern comes round again.
A pattern of n notes passes through n offsets and returns to unison.

## 35.3 Ostinato layers

Repeating cells of different lengths, played together, never settle into one pattern for a long time. Switch layers on one at a time.

::: {.pt data-pt="layers"}
:::

## Practice

1. A pattern has 5 notes. How many different offsets can the second voice have in stepped phasing, counting unison?
2. If it plays each offset for 8 cycles, how many cycles until the voices are back in unison?
3. With cells of 3, 4, 5 and 7 notes, after how many notes do all four line up again?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

1. 5 (0 to 4 notes ahead).
2. 5 &times; 8 = 40 cycles.
3. The least common multiple, 3&times;4&times;5&times;7 = 420 notes (4 = 2&times;2, but the others have no common factor with it).
:::
